title: DID GOD CREATE EVIL?
paragraphs:
DID GOD CREATE EVIL?
The Verse That Terrified Generations… and the Truth Most People Never Heard
There are verses in Scripture that comfort people.
Then there are verses that stop people cold.
Verses that sound like they could shatter everything believers think they know about God.
In the King James Version, God says:
“I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the Lord do all these things.”
For centuries, skeptics have weaponized those words.
Others read the verse once… then bury the discomfort deep enough to never revisit it again.
Because if God created evil… then what does that mean?
Did God create Satan to become evil?
And if God is holy… how can evil come from Him?
This is not a shallow question.
This is the kind of question people cry about at 2 a.m.
The kind of question whispered after funerals.
The kind of question asked by exhausted believers trying to reconcile God’s goodness with the horrors they’ve survived.
And maybe the hardest part is this:
The Bible never runs away from difficult questions.
God never panics when humans wrestle.
But to understand Isaiah 45:7 correctly, we must step into the language, culture, theology, and context the verse was originally written in.
Because one mistranslated English word has confused millions.
And the truth hiding underneath it is breathtaking.
The Hebrew text of Isaiah 45:7 reads:
“יוֹצֵר אוֹר וּבוֹרֵא חֹשֶׁךְ עֹשֶׂה שָׁלוֹם וּבוֹרֵא רָע”
“Yotzer or u-vorei choshekh, oseh shalom u-vorei ra.”
“Forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating ra.”
The entire controversy revolves around one Hebrew word:
Most people assume “ra” always means moral evil.
But Hebrew is deeper than that.
The Hebrew word “ra” has a broad semantic range.
Depending on context, it can mean:
• calamity • disaster • distress • adversity • sorrow • affliction • misery • trouble • judgment • harmful consequences
Sometimes it refers to moral evil.
And Isaiah 45 is not discussing moral corruption.
It is discussing God’s sovereignty over nations, kings, war, judgment, restoration, and history itself.
In modern translations, Isaiah 45:7 is more accurately rendered:
But because the original Hebrew context was restored.
God is not claiming to manufacture moral wickedness.
He is declaring absolute sovereignty over judgment and national calamity.
Isaiah 45 is addressed primarily to Cyrus, the Persian king God would use to judge nations and later allow Israel’s restoration.
“Does disaster come to a city, unless the Lord has done it?”
“Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come?”
Not moral corruption originating inside God.
Because Scripture is crystal clear about God’s moral nature.
“God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all.”
“Ὁ Θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν, καὶ σκοτία ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδεμία.”
“Ho Theos phos estin, kai skotia en auto ouk estin oudemia.”
“God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man.”
The Greek word for evil there is:
“You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong…”
So the Bible cannot contradict itself.
If God is perfectly holy… then Isaiah 45:7 cannot mean God creates moral evil.
But that still leaves another difficult question.
If God did not create evil… where did evil come from?
The answer is both terrifying and deeply personal.
Evil is not a created substance.
It is the corruption of what was originally good.
Darkness is not a created thing.
Darkness is the absence of light.
Cold is the absence of heat.
Rot is the corruption of life.
Evil is the rebellion against God’s goodness.
Scripture teaches that God created angels good.
“You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.”
“I will make myself like the Most High.”
Then humanity repeated the same rebellion in Eden.
Genesis never portrays God injecting Adam and Eve with evil.
And love without choice is not love.
Real obedience requires the possibility of rejection.
That possibility opened the door for sin.
And humanity walked through it willingly.
Because people often want evil explained in abstraction.
But Scripture keeps bringing it back to the human heart.
“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts…”
Humanity does not merely encounter evil.
The Bible refuses to let humanity pretend innocence.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Which means the question is not merely:
“Why would a holy God still love people capable of it?”
And this is where the Gospel explodes with unbearable beauty.
Because Christianity is not the story of a God who created evil.
It is the story of a holy God stepping into the devastation evil caused.
Jesus did not watch suffering from a distance.
The cross is God confronting evil head-on.
The Son of God stepped into human violence.
The greatest proof that God did not create moral evil is the cross itself.
Yet even there, God remained sovereign.
Acts 2:23 says Jesus was delivered up according to:
“the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.”
God remains sovereign over history without becoming morally corrupt.
And some people struggle with that tension.
Because they want a God who removes all possibility of evil immediately.
But that would also remove freedom.
The same free will that allows rebellion also allows repentance.
The same mouth that lies can worship.
The same heart that hated can be transformed.
The same sinner that fell can be redeemed.
That is the entire miracle of grace.
And maybe this hits differently when suffering becomes personal.
Maybe you buried someone too early.
Maybe evil did not feel philosophical to you.
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
The Bible is brutally honest about pain.
But it never concludes God is evil.
Instead, it reveals a God patient enough to allow freedom temporarily while preparing final justice eternally.
Revelation promises a coming day where evil ends completely.
The story is not over yet.
Because some people judge God before reading the final chapter.
But until then, humanity stands in a terrifying tension:
We want justice for evil done against us.
But mercy for evil done by us.
And only the Gospel resolves both.
At the cross, justice and mercy kissed.
This is why the question “Did God create evil?” cannot merely become an intellectual debate.
Because every human being must answer another question:
“What will I do with my own sin?”
The Gospel does not simply explain evil.
Then offers redemption through Jesus Christ.
And maybe the most haunting truth of all is this:
Many people spend their entire lives accusing God of evil while secretly refusing to surrender their own.
Especially when nobody else sees the thoughts.
But the Gospel still reaches there.
No matter how far someone ran.
No matter how dirty the past became.
No matter how many nights were wasted.
“Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”
Not permission to continue in sin.
But proof that Christ is greater than the wreckage.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years angry at God because of what evil did to your life.
You are not weak for wrestling.
But do not mistake human rebellion for God’s character.
The empty tomb reveals His character.
God did not create moral evil.
But He did create a rescue plan before humanity even realized it would need saving.
Because the story of Scripture is not:
And God came to save humanity anyway.
That is the scandal of grace.
That is the unbearable mercy of Christ.
And maybe this article exposed questions you buried for years.
Maybe it confronted hidden anger toward God.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if someone you love is wrestling with doubt, suffering, anger, trauma, or confusion about God… share this with them.
One day every hidden thing will stand before perfect holiness.
